problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: ‘Recipe Swap & Cook-Together’: residents bring one pantry staple and a family recipe; the six volunteers supply basic utensils from home. In the empty room they form rotating pairs to cook two dishes, sharing stories behind each recipe. After 90 minutes, everyone tastes and votes for the most memorable tale. Cost is under 50 euros for condiments and cleaning supplies; start next weekend with flyers at the bakery and library.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill Relay." In session one, each adult writes one step of the target skill on a card. The group arranges cards into a logical sequence, then practices in pairs using only the cards. In session two, pairs teach another pair, refining the sequence. Success is observable when every quartet can perform the skill unprompted and the final sequence matches expert criteria.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: “Story Swap & Seed” – in one afternoon residents each bring one small plant cutting and a 2-minute story about their street. Pairs trade cuttings while retelling the story; after three rounds, everyone plants the new cutting together in a communal pot kept in the room. €30 buys soil, pots, labels; remaining €270 covers snacks. Starts next Saturday; no skills needed.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Host a 90-minute ‘Story Swap & Seed Share’ on the first Saturday. Each of six volunteers brings one personal object under 300 g and one seed or bulb. In pairs, participants trade 3-minute stories tied to their object, then exchange seeds with a pledge to meet again when the plant blooms. A €20 whiteboard, €15 marker set, €10 snacks and €5 printed pledge cards total €50; remaining €250 stays unspent. The room becomes a rotating gallery of sprouting plants and signed cards, turning strangers into recurring neighbours.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: ‘Skill Relay.’ Week 1: each of 12 adults brings one real-life example of the target skill and, in 60 minutes, rotates through 3-minute micro-teaching stations, writing key steps on index cards. Week 2: pairs swap cards, attempt the skill live, then co-author a single one-page cheat-sheet. Success is observable when the cheat-sheet is posted and 9 of 12 can demonstrate the skill correctly to a librarian in under five minutes.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a 90-minute ‘Fix-or-Find’ circle: participants bring one broken item, list its material, and vote on repair, reuse, or recycle. A 15-minute skills-share demo precedes small-team attempts using shared tools. A ‘Triage Card’ on each item records decision and reason, preventing endless tinkering. Success is measured by the percentage of items diverted from landfill (target 70 %) and anonymous exit slips rating confidence gained on a 1-5 scale.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Skill Swap Chain. Session 1: each adult writes one practical skill they know and one they want on cards. Cards are shuffled and redistributed. In pairs, the expert demonstrates the skill for 20 minutes using only gestures and notes; the learner then re-teaches it. Session 2: learners pair with a new partner and teach the skill they just acquired, receiving immediate feedback. Success is observable because every participant must demonstrate the newly learned skill to their second partner within the hour, creating a visible chain of transmission without external resources.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Host a one-day 'Fix, Swap & Share' pop-up: participants triage each broken object as 'repair,' 'parts,' or 'scrap.' One table hosts a simple jig for gluing, taping, and sewing. A visible whiteboard lists each item’s fate so no repair is promised. Safeguard: pre-marked 'hazard' bin for sharp or toxic pieces. Success metric: count of objects diverted from landfill and number of first-time fixers who complete a repair, tallied at end-of-day.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Weekly "Story Swap & Supper": six volunteers cook a simple €300 communal meal in the empty room; each brings a personal object. Over two hours participants eat, share the story behind their item, then pair newcomers for a 10-minute follow-up chat scheduled within a week. Reusable name tags and a shared contact sheet ensure ongoing connections. No specialist kit needed, starts next Saturday.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Open Repair Jam: 1) Circle objects on table; each participant picks one they want to try. 2) 20-min mini-clinic: pair novices with confident neighbors; tools shared. 3) Items that stall after 30 min move to ‘parts station’—components harvested for other fixes. Safeguard: pre-agreed 30-min timer prevents over-investment. Success measure: tally fixed items plus new skills named by each participant at close. Waste reduced by reuse of parts; participation encouraged by choice and peer support.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Repair Potluck: participants bring one broken item and a dish. A 90-minute circuit of three stations—diagnose, attempt-fix, or harvest-parts—lets people rotate freely. A “finished or donated” bin prevents hoarding. Success is measured by items leaving in working order plus number of new skill-sharing pairs observed. A volunteer time-keeper ends each station promptly to keep energy high.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: ‘Story-Swap Picnic’: Residents bring one personal object and a 300-word written anecdote. In pairs they swap objects and read each other’s stories aloud. After 20 minutes, pairs reform to share one surprising connection found. A volunteer hosts a 10-minute closing circle where everyone states one new fact learned about a neighbor. Six volunteers handle setup, timing and cleanup. Venue: empty room plus adjacent lawn. Cost: 60 € for simple sandwiches and water; remainder for printed name tags and string to hang objects. Starts Saturday after next; no specialist gear needed. Lasting connections emerge from shared vulnerability and repeated name-face-story recall.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: “Story-Swap Picnic” begins in two weeks on a Saturday afternoon in the empty room. Six volunteers each invite two neighbours they barely know, forming 18 initial participants. Everyone brings one dish or drink under 5 € (total budget 90 € for cups, napkins, water). Participants draw lots to pair with someone new every 15 minutes; each pair swaps a two-minute personal story prompted by a printed question card (budget 10 € for printing). After six rotations the whole group shares one takeaway aloud. Remaining 200 € covers a reusable banner and two folding tables borrowed from the town hall. The low-cost, recurring format encourages follow-up meet-ups and creates an expanding contact web without specialist gear.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Hold a 3-hour Repair Swap Circle. Participants sort items into “fix,” “parts,” or “art” piles. One volunteer demonstrates a safe fix on the table; others work in pairs. Safeguard: a first-aid kit and a 10-minute safety briefing. Success is measured by counting items diverted from trash and by anonymous exit cards rating enjoyment 1-5.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill Relay." Participants split into pairs. In hour one each pair receives one short written segment of the skill and must master it using only their notes, then teach it to another pair. In hour two pairs merge into fours and teach their combined segments onward until every quartet demonstrates the full skill. Success is observed when each final group performs the complete skill in under five minutes without notes. This works because peer teaching multiplies repetition, immediate feedback, and accountability while the relay structure prevents anyone from skipping steps.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Process: 1) 15-minute circle where each participant chooses one object and states one reason it still matters. 2) Two-hour stations: glue/tape, sewing, sanding, and ‘creative reuse’ for pieces beyond repair. 3) Table becomes display area; objects with no safe fix are photographed and logged for a future craft swap. Safeguard: color-coded tags—green for usable, red for unsafe—checked by two people before any item leaves. Success: at end, count green-tagged items returned to owners plus a one-question exit slip (1–5) on ‘I felt welcome.’ Target: ≥10 green items and average score ≥4.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Fix-or-Fabricate Circle: 1) Participants sort the 20 objects into “fix,” “repurpose,” “parts,” or “scrap.” 2) Two-person teams attempt repairs with table/tools for 20 min; unfixables become raw material for quick creative builds. 3) Safeguard: pre-agreed “no-blame” exit—any stalled item moves to scrap without judgment. 4) Success check: count repaired items + new creations and brief 3-question survey on confidence gained. Waste is diverted, participation stays voluntary.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: 'Chain-Learn'—each adult masters one micro-skill, teaches the next person in a live 15-minute relay, then rotates. Stationery becomes visual cheat-sheets passed along the chain. After two sessions the group performs the full skill in sequence; success is observable when every participant completes their segment correctly without notes and the chain finishes under 10 minutes.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Peer-Teaching Circles: Twelve adults form four trios. Each trio receives one plain index card naming one sequential step of the skill (e.g., Step 1, Step 2). In Hour 1, trios use only stationery to teach their step to the other groups through drawings, gestures, or short skits; listeners must reproduce the step on paper. In Hour 2, trios rotate and repeat. Success is observable when each participant can correctly order, explain, and physically demonstrate all twelve steps in sequence without cards.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Skill: origami crane with hidden pocket for a note. Hour 1: each person receives one pre-creased square. In pairs, they silently watch then mirror each fold, writing the step on the shared sheet. Hour 2: pairs swap partners, teach the full sequence without talking, then assemble a twelve-crane mobile. Observable success: the mobile hangs evenly, each crane opens to show a legible note, and every participant can fold one crane from memory in under three minutes.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Repair Jam: 1) Two-hour drop-in. 2) Objects sorted into “Try,” “Parts,” “Show-&-Tell.” 3) Mixed-skill pairs use basic tools; a posted “Stop Rule” halts work if repair exceeds 20 min or safety risk. 4) Unfinished items become art or spare-parts sculpture. 5) Success measured by: ≥60 % of participants report higher repair confidence on exit cards and ≥30 % of objects diverted from landfill (weighed before/after).

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each broken object with a card noting its story and a repair wish. They choose one of three stations: quick-fix, creative-upcycle, or story-display. The table becomes a shared workbench; tools and glue are pooled. A posted ‘triage rule’ lets anyone set an object aside if it seems unsafe or too complex, preventing frustration. After two hours, each station shares one result and one lesson learned. Success is measured by counting how many objects leave with a new purpose or documented story rather than landfill, plus a show-of-hands poll on whether participants felt welcome and willing to return.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill Relay". Each adult picks a sub-skill (e.g., tying a knot). In hour 1, pairs swap 5-min demos until everyone has tried every step; each notes one strength/weakness on sticky notes. In hour 2, groups of three reconstruct the full sequence from notes, then perform the skill while the others score the sequence with checkmarks. Success is observable: final checklist scores rise from first to second run and every learner signs their name next to a completed checklist.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: “Story Threads” night: six volunteers collect 30-second voice clips from neighbors on phones about a shared childhood meal. Over one week, they stitch clips into a 12-minute audio quilt, burn it to a €25 CD, and host a free listening party with €50 snacks. Each participant receives a printed track list noting the storyteller’s first name and dish, sparking follow-up kitchen swaps. Starts in 10 days; needs only phones, speakers, paper, and goodwill.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Fix-or-Find Circle: 1) Spread 20 broken items on one table. 2) Each participant chooses an object and tries to repair it for 10 minutes with hand tools. 3) If stuck, label it “Parts” or “Inspire,” then return it. 4) Others may adopt or harvest labeled items. 5) After 60 minutes, sort survivors: repaired, reusable parts, or recycle. Time-keeper and posted timer prevent endless tinkering. Success = (repaired + parts reused)/20; aim ≥30 % diversion and ≥75 % of people handling ≥1 object.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Skill Swap Chain: Adults each write one practical skill they know and one they want. Cards are shuffled; everyone receives a fresh card. In Session 1, pairs teach each other 20 minutes then rotate twice. Session 2, each person demonstrates the newly learned skill for 3 minutes. Success is observable because every participant must both teach and perform a new skill publicly, providing immediate, visible evidence of transfer.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a free community recipe-swap picnic in the empty room. Residents bring one homemade dish and its story on index cards. Volunteers label tables, supply water, napkins, and borrow six chairs. Pairs rotate every 15 minutes to taste and chat. After two hours, everyone writes one new contact detail on a shared wall poster. Budget covers €50 for basic supplies; leftover funds buy reusable name tags. Event scheduled for next Saturday afternoon, no skills or equipment needed.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Skill Swap Chain. Session 1: Each adult writes one practical skill they know on a card and one they want to learn. Cards are shuffled; everyone receives a new card. Pairs form and teach each other for 20 minutes, then rotate. Session 2: Each person demonstrates the skill they learned to the whole group for 3 minutes. Success is observable because every participant must both teach and perform a new skill in front of peers, creating immediate, visible evidence of learning transfer.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Story Tiles: residents bring one object and a 60-word story about it. Volunteers create a shared timeline on the floor using tape. Each person places their object, shares the story and ties a ribbon to two others’ objects that resonate. After 90 minutes they photograph the web and plan a monthly reunion to swap new stories. Resources: tape, ribbons, phone camera, free room; zero cost beyond existing items.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Upcycle Circle: Lay out the 20 broken objects and table. Each participant chooses one item and a simple repair or repurposing task they feel confident attempting. Tools and supplies remain communal; a “Help Wanted” sign lets anyone request a quick tip. A 30-minute “show-and-tell” closes the session. Safeguard: any item deemed unsafe or unfixable moves straight to a labelled recycling bin. Success measured by count of objects diverted from landfill plus brief anonymous exit slips rating enjoyment and learning (1-5).

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighbors gather in the empty room for a 90-minute "Story-and-Skill Swap" on the second Saturday. Each of six volunteers brings one inexpensive, familiar object (photo, recipe, tool) and shares its story in three minutes; listeners note one detail they wish to learn. Pairs then schedule a 30-minute home visit within ten days to exchange the skill. A shared Google Doc records contacts and dates, costing under 300 euros for tea, biscuits and printing.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a 300-euro 'Story-Plate Picnic' in the empty room. Buy picnic blankets, paper plates, markers, and snacks. Each of the six volunteers pairs with three unknown residents. Pairs draw or write a short personal memory on their plate, swap plates, and share the story behind it. After 30 minutes, rotate to new pairs. Plates become take-home mementos. Total cost: blankets 50 €, plates/markers 30 €, snacks 120 €, small thank-you cards 20 €, contingency 80 €. No specialist gear needed; activity starts next Saturday.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: ‘Skill Chain Relay’. In meeting one, the twelve learners each receive one unique step of a chosen practical skill (e.g., basic bicycle repair) on an index card. In pairs they teach each other their step, then combine pairs to teach groups of four, building a chain until everyone knows all twelve steps. In meeting two, the group performs the full skill in real time, each member responsible for their original step. Success is observable when the bicycle is repaired, tested, and rolls smoothly within the hour.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: ‘Story-Seed Exchange’: volunteers host a free, two-hour indoor storytelling circle in the empty room. Each of six participants brings one small personal object and a 2-minute story; listeners jot kind notes on cards. After round-robin sharing, cards are swapped and later mailed, turning acquaintances into pen-pals. Budget: 25 € postcards + 10 € tea, rest for flyers and two-week promotion via town hall and library. No equipment needed beyond chairs and a kettle.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: 'Skill Relay'. Session 1: group lists target skill steps on cards. Each learner secretly masters one step using the cards. Session 2: learners form a circle, demonstrating their step in sequence; peers replicate immediately, correcting errors on the spot. Success observable via final flawless group performance and signed checklist of all steps.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: ‘Story-Exchange Circle’: Volunteers host six residents for a 90-minute free event in the empty room. Each brings one meaningful object or photo. In pairs they swap items and explain their story (5 min each). After three rotations, the group reconvenes; every participant shares one new connection they discovered. Resources: six chairs, sticky notes for name tags, one kettle for free tea. Starts next Saturday; no cost beyond 10 euros for tea and biscuits.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Fix-or-Find Circle: 1) Arrange 20 objects and tools on a table. 2) Each participant claims one item and attempts repair for 10 minutes. 3) If stuck, they tag it “Parts” or “Inspire” and return it. 4) Others may adopt or harvest tagged items. 5) After 60 min, sort survivors: repaired, reusable parts, recycle. Safeguard: visible timer plus a rotating time-keeper ends sessions promptly. Success metric: (repaired + reused parts)/20 ≥30 % diversion and ≥75 % of participants handle at least one object.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Story-Swap Picnic: residents pair up, each brings one personal object and a 2-minute story. Every 5 minutes pairs swap objects and retell the story to a new partner. After three rounds, the whole group shares one surprising connection. Open to all ages, 20–40 people, no RSVP. Use the empty room or a park. Six volunteers time rounds and greet. 300 € covers snacks and name-tags. Starts next Saturday afternoon, lasts two hours, no specialist gear.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Skill Swap Chain. Session 1: Each adult writes one practical skill they know and one they want to learn on separate cards. Cards are shuffled; everyone receives a new card. In pairs, the expert teaches their skill for 20 minutes using only demonstration and note-taking; the learner then teaches it back. Session 2: Learners pair with a new partner and teach the skill they just acquired, receiving feedback. Success is observable because each person must demonstrate the newly learned skill to their second partner within the hour, creating a visible chain of transmission without external resources.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a free ‘Story-Swap Picnic’ in the empty room. Volunteers collect household objects from residents beforehand. On the day, each participant places one item in a circle and briefly explains its personal story. Listeners may ask respectful questions. Items are swapped at the end so everyone leaves with a new keepsake. Budget covers simple snacks and printed name tags. The shared objects and stories create immediate common ground, while the tangible keepsakes give ongoing conversation starters, fostering lasting ties among strangers.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: 'Skill Relay.' Session 1: Pair learners, each receives one unique segment of the skill. They master it using trial-and-error, then teach it to their partner. Session 2: Pairs merge into a circle; each person demonstrates their segment while the group practices together. Success: In final round, every learner performs the full skill without notes; observers note zero errors per segment across all participants.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a twice-weekly 'Recipe Swap & Cook' in the empty room. Each volunteer brings one family dish, its story, and one low-cost ingredient. Participants cook together, share the meal, and exchange contact details. A simple roster and €50 for shared staples cover two weeks; the rest of the budget buys cleaning supplies and printed name tags. After the final session, a shared online photo album keeps the new connections alive.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Fix-or-Find Circle. Lay out the 20 objects; each participant selects one and tags it “Repair,” “Parts,” or “Story.” Run three 20-minute micro-workshops in parallel—basic soldering, gluing, sewing—led by confident participants. Unrepaired items move to a Harvest Station where usable parts are logged in a shared inventory and husks go to local recycling. Safeguard: 10-minute safety brief plus one adult supervisor per station. Success: count items diverted from landfill (target ≥12) and a post-event survey showing ≥70 % of participants report higher repair confidence.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill Relay." Session 1: Each learner researches one segment of the skill with library books, then teaches it to a partner in 5-minute bursts; partners rotate every 10 minutes until all segments are covered. Session 2: Teams perform a timed relay: each member must demonstrate their segment sequentially to the group, with peers scoring clarity and accuracy on simple checklists. Success is observable via completed checklists, time logs, and a final group performance judged by a librarian for completeness and accuracy.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Peer-teaching rotation: learners form four trios. In meeting 1, each person secretly practices a 3-step micro-skill from the practical goal for 15 min, then teaches it to the other two in 5 min each; observers note timing and errors on shared paper. Trios swap and repeat. In meeting 2, trios merge into one group; each learner performs the full skill once while the others score it 1-5 on accuracy and speed. Average score ≥4 indicates mastery.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each adult draws a two-step skill diagram on index cards. Pair up, swap cards, and silently perform the steps while the partner watches. The watcher scores 1-3 accuracy; pairs swap roles. All gather and the highest-scoring pairs teach their step to the room. Success is visible: each card has three independent scores, and final group performance shows measurable improvement between rounds.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: Each adult chooses one step of the skill, practices it alone for 10 minutes, then demonstrates it to a partner who times and notes what worked. In hour two, pairs merge into groups of four, teach the four steps as a sequence, and refine together. Success is observable when each group performs the full skill in under five minutes with zero prompting and each member can explain any step on request.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants each bring one page describing a single practical skill step they know. Over two hours, they rotate in pairs, teaching their step then learning the next, using only pen-and-paper notes. After each round, learners initial the page they now understand. At the end, each person’s sheet shows ten signatures beside ten distinct steps, proving collective mastery without a teacher or digital tools.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Story-Swap: In the empty room, set up a circle of chairs and a simple table with tea and cookies (under 50 €). Over two hours, each resident shares a 5-minute personal story about a turning point in their life. Listeners then pair up for 10-minute one-on-one chats to exchange reactions and contact details. A volunteer runs a 5-minute closing round where everyone states one new thing learned about someone else. Materials: paper, pens, kettle. This requires no specialist equipment and can start next weekend.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Invite residents to a one-day ‘Re-Pair’ pop-up: participants sort the 20 objects into three labeled zones—Fix, Adapt, Recycle—using the table as a shared workspace. Anyone may attempt a repair, but the rule is ‘document, try, decide.’ A volunteer records each item’s fate on a visible tally sheet. Safeguard: a posted time-limit (90 min) and a ‘no-tool’ rule for children. Success metric: at least 70 % of objects diverted from landfill and a signed feedback card from each participant confirming they learned one new skill or felt included.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Form a Repair-Swap Circle: 1) Lay out objects and vote 'fix', 'repurpose', or 'parts'. 2) Pair confident with less-confident neighbors; assign 30-minute stations. 3) Use a shared 'parts tray' to cannibalize irreparables. 4) Safeguard: mark any sharp-edge item 'hands-off' and store it. 5) Success metric: tally objects leaving in usable form versus landfill; aim for ≥60% diversion and ≥80% participant satisfaction via quick exit poll.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Host a 90-minute 'Repair or Reimagine' pop-up: 1) Sort objects into repairable and re-purpose piles. 2) Two-station circuit—repair bench (tools, glue, tape) and reimagine table (paint, fabric scraps). 3) Participants rotate every 15 min, guided by a volunteer coach. 4) Safeguard: red tape marks any sharp or electrical hazard; only adults handle these items. 5) Success metric: count objects that leave useful or decorative; target 60 % diverted from trash, recorded on a shared whiteboard. End with a 5-min circle sharing one takeaway each.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Story-Swap Picnic: residents pair up, bring one personal object and a 2-minute story. Pairs swap objects and retell the story to new partners every 5 minutes for three rounds; the whole group then shares one surprising connection. Open to all ages, 20–40 people, no RSVP. Free park or empty room, six volunteers as greeters/time-keepers, 300 € for snacks and name-tags. Two-hour session next Saturday afternoon; no specialist gear.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Two-week 'Story Swap & Map' project: Volunteers collect one short, anonymous anecdote from each resident about a favourite local spot. Budget buys index cards, markers and a large wall map. Residents pin cards to their chosen locations. Weekly drop-in sessions let people read stories, match faces to pins, and add replies. After two weeks a shared coffee closes the loop, turning strangers into neighbours via visible, lasting connections.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill-Chain Relay". Assign each participant one 5-minute segment of the skill. In hour one, pairs teach their segment to each other, then rotate until everyone has taught and learned all segments. Hour two, groups of three reconstruct the full sequence from memory, then the whole group performs it together. Observable success: a single, uninterrupted 3-minute demonstration of the complete skill performed without notes or prompting.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Twelve adults form four trios. Each trio receives one skill step, a pencil, and paper. In round one, the trio teaches its step to the other three trios, using only gestures, diagrams, and written notes. Round two: trios swap steps and repeat. Round three: everyone practices the full sequence together, noting gaps on a shared wall chart. Success is observed when each adult can demonstrate the complete skill without notes and the chart lists no unresolved gaps after two hours.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Peer-led skill swap: learners choose one practical skill each (e.g., basic bicycle repair). Session 1: in pairs, one person demonstrates a 5-minute segment while the other records steps with pen and index cards. Roles reverse. Cards are shuffled and redistributed. Session 2: everyone teaches the segment on their new card to a fresh partner, then demonstrates the full skill to the group. Success is observable when each adult can perform the complete skill and coach another learner without notes.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Fix-or-Not Circle: 1) Quick triage—sort objects into ‘Try’, ‘Parts’, or ‘Pass’. 2) Rotating teams of two (one confident, one learning) attempt 15-minute repairs on Try items using table and hand tools. 3) Safeguard: a visible ‘retire’ bin prevents unsafe fixes. 4) Success measured by percentage of objects diverted from landfill and number of first-time participants who return next month.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants bring one broken item to a shared table. Each person labels the object with its perceived repairability (easy, tricky, hopeless) using colored stickers. Groups of three rotate every 15 minutes, attempting only easy-labeled items first with basic tools. A “triage board” records progress and time spent. Items left unrepaired after two rotations are dismantled for parts or art. Safeguard: a 10-minute “pause bell” allows anyone to stop if frustrated. Success measured by number of items diverted from landfill and average participant-reported confidence on a 1–5 sticky note collected at exit.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Story-Swap Picnic: Residents bring one personal object and a two-minute story. Six volunteers borrow picnic blankets, buy €50 snacks, and set up a free park corner. Pairs rotate every ten minutes for three rounds; groups of six then co-create a one-page “town memory map” on large paper. Maps are photocopied (€20) and mailed to participants, giving each a tangible keepsake and contact list. €70 total spend, three days’ prep, runs one Saturday afternoon within two weeks.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood Fix-It Lab: 1) Label each item with its story. 2) 20-min skill-share circles teach tool basics and quick diagnostics. 3) Pairs choose one object to attempt; if parts are missing or unsafe, move it to the communal art table instead of forcing repair. 4) A visible ‘risk card’ checklist (gloves, goggles, sharp-edge test) serves as safeguard. 5) Success is tallied by smiles on exit survey and count of salvaged or repurposed items; goal is ≥50% engagement and zero injuries.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Fix-or-Find Circle: lay out objects; each participant tags one "Repair," "Parts," or "Story." 20-minute parallel micro-workshops teach basic soldering/gluing/sewing. Unrepaired items move to Harvest Station for parts logging; husks recycle. 10-min safety brief, one adult per station. Success: count items diverted from landfill (target ≥12) and ≥70 % post-survey confidence rise.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: "Skill Swap Circuit". Learners form pairs and choose one practical skill each to teach in 15-minute micro-lessons. After two rounds, pairs swap partners and repeat, ensuring four exposures. Each learner logs one observable action they performed and one they received on a shared wall chart. Success is observable via the completed chart, where every participant has at least four logged actions by session two. The method works because repeated teaching solidifies knowledge, peer modeling builds confidence, and visible logs create accountability without external resources.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Process: ‘Fix-or-Find’ pop-up. 1) 10-min safety demo using table. 2) Participants choose 1-2 objects; log issue, confidence, and decide repair, repurpose, or recycle. 3) 30-min hands-on slots with shared tools; volunteers help peers. 4) ‘Unfixables’ table becomes art or spare-parts display. Safeguard: color-coded tags prevent electrical work. Success: count objects diverted from landfill and post-event survey on skill confidence (target 70 % report gain).

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Organize a 90-minute Repair-or-Repurpose Circle: 1) Lay out the 20 objects and invite each participant to choose one. 2) Provide a 20-minute triage station with basic tools and a simple checklist (needs part? skill beyond group? sentimental?). Objects needing unavailable parts move to the Repurpose table. 3) Pairs attempt fixes; unfixable items are disassembled for parts or turned into art/supplies. 4) Safeguard: a posted “No blame, no guarantees” sign and a volunteer time-keeper who halts work after 30 minutes. 5) Success measured by tallying fixed items, created artworks, and exit sticky-note ratings (1–5) of participation comfort—target 70 % positive.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Pairs create a 12-step "skill card" by each writing one step on an index card, passing it, and adding the next step until complete. In session two, teams test cards by performing the skill while peers observe and score each step visible on the card. Success is measured by 80% of steps completed correctly without prompts.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A Repair-Circle: 1) Participants briefly share one story about each broken item. 2) Group votes, by show of hands, which 10 items are worth a first look. 3) Three repair stations are set up; each station has one tool kit and one confident helper. 4) A 25-minute timer limits work; if progress stalls, the item is tagged “parts only.” 5) A visible whiteboard tallies rescued items vs. parts harvested. 6) Safeguard: a red card can be raised by any participant to stop work on an object that poses safety risks. 7) Success metric: at least 50 % of selected items leave either repaired or cleanly disassembled for recycling, and every participant reports trying at least one new skill.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Create a ‘Story Jar’ evening: residents bring one personal object and a short written anecdote. In pairs they exchange items, guess the story, then reveal the truth. After 20 minutes they switch. A simple rota keeps six volunteers hosting rounds; each hosts once. Use the empty room, six chairs, paper, pens, jars from home. Total cost under 20 euros for refreshments and name tags. Pairs rotate until everyone has met, forging quick, memorable links without specialist gear.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A two-week ‘Story Circle & Seed Swap’ in the empty room. Day 1: six volunteers each bring one small plant cutting or seed packet and a 2-minute personal story. Participants pair up, exchange cuttings and swap stories, then write one question on a shared board. Over the next 12 days, pairs meet daily for 20 minutes to tend the plants, answer one board question, and add a new one. On day 14 everyone gathers to pot the grown plants together and keep the board as an ongoing conversation wall. Resources: 6 cuttings, paper, markers, water, 300 € for snacks and basic pots. No specialist gear needed.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Community Memory Mural: six volunteers host a 2-hour storytelling-and-collage night in the empty room. Each resident brings one personal item or photo (or draws one). Participants share a two-minute story about it, then glue or tape it onto a large donated roll of paper, forming a collective mural. Budget covers tape, glue sticks, markers, snacks and drinks. Sign-up sheets collect contact details so neighbors can arrange follow-up meet-ups. The mural stays on display for a month, giving newcomers a visual introduction to their neighbors and a tangible reason to reconnect.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Story-Swap Picnic uses an empty room as indoor backup. Residents bring one personal object and a 2-minute story. Six volunteers borrow blankets, spend €50 on snacks, and €20 on photocopies. Pairs rotate every 10 minutes for three rounds; then groups of six co-create a 1-page town memory map. The map is copied and mailed with contact details, giving each participant a keepsake and future connections. Total €70, 3-day prep, one Saturday afternoon within two weeks.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: One-day Repair-and-Share Drop-in: neighbors bring the 20 broken objects to a public table. A short safety demo covers tool use; each item is tagged green (quick fix), yellow (learn-together) or red (parts donor). Volunteers pick green/yellow items; red items are disassembled for parts or art. A running tally board shows repairs completed and materials saved. Safeguard: red-tag items may only be disassembled after two people agree repair is impractical. Success is measured by tally count plus a one-question exit poll: “Would you try fixing something else?”
